title: How a Neural Network Learns Part 2

scenes.text: In part one, we learned that training means finding good weights. [1] But a big network has billions of weights, so how does it find good ones? [2] In part two, let's understand the loss, and gradient descent.

First, the network needs a way to know how wrong it is. [1] That's called the loss, a single number that measures the mistake. [2] A big loss means a bad answer, [3] a small loss means a good answer, [4] and training tries to make the loss as small as possible.

data.definition: A single number that measures how wrong the network's answer is.

scenes.text: Here's an example. The network sees a photo of a cat. [1] It guesses, 30 percent cat, and 70 percent dog. [2] The right answer is 100 percent cat, so the loss is high. [3] After learning a little, it guesses 90 percent cat, and the loss drops.

So how does it adjust the weights? With gradient descent. [1] Imagine you're on a foggy hill at night, and you want to reach the bottom. [2] You feel which way the ground slopes down, [3] take a small step that way, [4] and repeat, until you reach the valley.

data.definition: Adjusting the weights in small steps, in the direction that reduces the loss, like walking downhill.

scenes.text: The size of each step is called the learning rate. [1] If the steps are too big, you leap over the valley, and bounce around forever. [2] If they're just right, you walk steadily down to the lowest point.

Here are four words from training. [1] An epoch, one full pass through all the training data. [2] A batch, a small group of examples looked at together. [3] The learning rate, which is the step size. [4] And convergence, when the loss stops improving, and training is done.

data.heading: Training words
terms: One full pass of the data
A small group at a time

scenes.text: Here's a common myth. [1] People think training finds the one perfect answer. [2] It usually finds a very good spot, not the perfect one. The landscape has many valleys, and a good valley is usually more than enough.

data.myth: Training finds the one perfect answer.
data.fact: It usually finds a very good spot, not the perfect one, and that's more than enough.
